mmjnb6.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday urged organizations to take steps to immediately update their Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) appliances and deployments to the latest version following the disclosure of an actively exploited vulnerability. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of authentication bypass impacting ICS versions 25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, and 22.8R2.4 and prior that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. "CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration," the agency said. The agency has since added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by October 16, 2026. CISA is also recommending that customers of affected ICS deployments review Ivanti's Connect Secure Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for patching guidance, cautioning that version 22.8 reaches end-of-life on January 31, 2027. "Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation," it added. In the event a compromise is detected, CISA is advising organizations to implement the following actions - Create a backup of the appliance configuration. Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. The development comes as Previdian disclosed that it has observed 105 exploitation attempts targeting its honeypot sensors as of October 14, 2026. The attack attempts have originated from 50 unique IP addresses geolocated to Singapore and the U.S. Some of the observed IP addresses are listed below - 216.73.160[.]59 216.73.160[.]61 216.73.160[.]210 45.8.19[.]111 According to Previdian founder and CEO, Ryan Dewhurst, threat actors are using the X-DSCGI-PATH header to reach an internal CGI handler and upload Perl scripts dressed up as ZIP files. The scripts return unique markers that determine whether remote code execution has succeeded. "We're seeing coordinated attempts to exploit this Ivanti vulnerability, but the payloads captured so far are primarily testing for code execution rather than deploying malware, or compromising the device," Dewhurst told The Hacker News. "However, full weaponized exploitation is likely to follow in the coming hours and days." In a separate report, Volexity said it first observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 on October 3, 2026, with a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576 leveraging it in conjunction with a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. UTA0576 is assessed to be driven by criminal motives rather than espionage. Following successful exploitation, the threat actor is said to have engaged in broad post-exploitation actions, including extracting credentials stored on the ICS VPN appliance, exfiltrating limited Active Directory metadata, deploying a Kerberos tool capable of Kerberoast attacks and credential testing, conducting host reconnaissance, LDAP packet capture, and dropping a Python LDAP tool to search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. "The recovered payloads demonstrate deliberate efforts to conceal malicious activity through selective log modification, removal of temporary execution artifacts, and restoration of altered system state," Volexity researchers Charlie Gardner, Sean Koessel, and Steven Adair said. "UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool." Threat intelligence company Defused Cyber has also confirmed active exploitation, stating its decoys "caught pre-disclosure exploitation we assess as CVE-2026-104935" in the wild starting October 1, 2026. "The root cause of the vulnerability is incredibly simple, with a single request containing a specially crafted 'X-DSCGI-PATH' header being all that is needed to bypass authentication and access sensitive functionality that otherwise should be restricted," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said. "Ivanti Connect Secure has long been a popular target for attackers, including ransomware gangs, and joins 14 other Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Connect Secure vulnerabilities on the CISA KEV list. Given the history, we expect exploitation to move incredibly quickly from targeted attacks to indiscriminate mass exploitation." It's essential that organizations running ICS patch immediately and investigate their appliances for signs of compromise, including identifying any inbound requests featuring an "X-DSCGI-PATH" header.

r737iu.text: A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine. The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead. The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023. The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix. The attack runs from the server side. The client has to upload a file of roughly 135KB over HTTP/2 to a server controlled by the attacker, and the server's certificate must pass the client's checks. libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for https:// URLs when the server offers it, and the library was built with HTTP/2 support. The flaw has shipped in every curl release since 8.12.0 in February 2025. No source reports attacks that use it. The reporter's HackerOne write-up, with the malicious server script and a Docker container described as reproducing the code execution, became public on October 14 with the advisory. What to Install, and What to Do Until Then Upgrade to 8.23.0 or apply the fix commit to a local build. curl's machine-readable advisory also lists fixed versions on three older branches, and the project said it would ship updated Rock-solid curl releases, its long-term-support line for customers with support contracts, in step with 8.23.0: curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0: upgrade to 8.23.0 8.14.x branch: 8.14.3 8.16.x branch: 8.16.2 8.20.x branch: 8.20.2 Debian 13 (trixie): 8.14.1-2+deb13u7 through DSA-6558-1, per Debian's tracker. Debian 12 (bookworm) does not carry the vulnerable code. The release fixes 24 CVEs in all. The other 23 are rated Low. If you cannot update yet, curl's advice is not to use HTTP/2. The --http1.1 option asks the tool for HTTP/1.1, and applications set CURLOPT_HTTP_VERSION to CURL_HTTP_VERSION_1_1. curl's documentation calls that setting a request, because an existing connection on another version may be reused. HTTP/2 support in libcurl is a build option. A build without it cannot negotiate HTTP/2, so it cannot reach the upload path the advisory describes. How a Hostile Server Turns the Bug Into Code Execution Daniel Stenberg, curl's lead developer, explained the bug in a post published with the release, and the public report lays out the code path. HTTP/2 carries several transfers over one connection, and libcurl tracks each transfer with an object it calls an easy handle. During an upload, the server stalls the transfer by setting the HTTP/2 window to zero, returning part of the response, and then resetting the stream while keeping the connection open. curl treats the reset as a reason to retry. In cleanup, curl first tells the HTTP/2 layer that the transfer is finished, then flushes the rest of the unsent upload into the same connection. With no transfer registered, those leftover bytes are read as a new request. The line pattern the reporter includes in the uploaded file makes them look like request lines. When they do, a new stream is opened that stores a pointer to the easy handle. The retry completes on a new HTTP/1.1 connection, and the application frees the handle. The old connection still holds the pointer and uses it when the server sends a frame on that stream, which can happen as the program exits. In the reporter's exploit, data the server sends lands in the memory the freed handle had used. A request that goes out leaks local addresses, which the server needs to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR). A function pointer in that memory is overwritten with bytes from the server, and curl then calls it. Code execution needs the attacker to know the target's exact curl version, architecture, libc allocator and heap layout, to keep two parallel transfers on the right timing, and to fit the payload into about 23 bytes, according to curl's advisory. "The most likely outcome of an attempted attack is rather just a crash," Stenberg wrote, putting the chance of success as slim. That is why curl graded the flaw High rather than Critical. curl uses four severity levels and publishes no CVSS score. The National Vulnerability Database had not analyzed the record as of October 14. The fix is a six-line reorder in lib/multi.c by Stefan Eissing. The HTTP/2 layer now gives up its references to the handle after the leftover upload data has been flushed, not before. The report reached curl on September 15 through HackerOne, and the security team confirmed it within hours, according to Stenberg. On October 7, the project pre-announced a High-severity fix for the next release, shortening its cycle from eight weeks to six. curl credits the finding to "Luna with Claude, Anthropic." Stenberg names the reporter as Luna Tong of Anthropic, says the finding came through the company's new OSS Scanner, and presumes its AI models were involved. Anthropic opened OSS Scanner on October 8 as an opt-in service that scans enrolled open-source projects with its models and emails the results without human review, each report with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch. The curl report came three weeks before that public launch. Anthropic's launch post quoted Stenberg saying the scanner had turned up "one of the worst curl vulnerabilities reported in the last few years," without naming one. The same maintainer wrote in July 2025 that about a fifth of curl's security submissions that year were what he called AI slop, and that only about one in twenty had proved genuine. curl has spent several years reducing the number of internal pointers to handles in favor of identifiers it looks up when needed, Stenberg wrote, and that is no guarantee against another use-after-free. curl calls the bug a mistake that a memory-safe language would likely have avoided, and the project does not plan to rewrite curl in one.

1szqej9.text: Cloned voices and synthetic video calls now show up in payment fraud, help desk resets, and access requests. A structured drill shows security teams exactly where verification breaks down, while nothing is at stake. The call comes in at 4:40 on a Friday. It's the CFO, or it sounds exactly like her, asking the controller to push a supplier payment out before the weekend because a deal closes Monday. She's traveling, she's rushed, and she apologizes for the bad connection. Ten minutes later an email lands with the wire details. A couple of years ago that scenario was a conference talk. Now it shows up in incident reports. In a 2025 Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, 62% said their organization had experienced at least one deepfake attack in the prior 12 months. In the same survey, 43% reported at least one deepfake audio call incident and 37% had run into deepfakes on video calls. And the wire is only the obvious ask. The same cloned voice can call the help desk to move an MFA token, or ask an identity admin to set up a new global admin ahead of an "audit." A fraudulent wire tends to surface at reconciliation. A quietly added admin account can sit there for months. Most organizations have a policy that says to verify unusual payment and access requests. Far fewer have checked whether that policy survives a phone call from someone who sounds like the person who signs off on everyone's paycheck. A deepfake readiness drill is how you find out, on your own schedule, with nothing real on the line. Why detection by ear falls short Security awareness training has long taught employees to look for tells. Awkward phrasing, an odd sender address, a link that doesn't match the text. Voice clones and real-time face swaps leave fewer of those tells every quarter. Asking people to hear the fake is asking a lot. In a May 2025 warning about AI-generated voice messages impersonating senior US officials, the FBI noted that cloned voices can sound nearly identical to the real person and told recipients to confirm identity by calling an independently sourced phone number before acting on anything. Security leaders already know this. In a January 2026 Osterman Research study of 128 US security and IT leaders, commissioned by IRONSCALES, 60% said they lacked confidence in their ability to counter deepfake attacks even with the training they already run. So the defense has to rest on process more than perception. If an employee runs the same verification step every time money, credentials, or permissions are involved, the quality of the fake stops mattering much. A drill tests whether that step actually happens when someone senior is leaning on them. Step 1. Map the voices worth cloning and the people worth calling Start with two short lists. The first is the people an attacker would impersonate. That means executives who can approve payments or direct staff (CEO, CFO, CIO, CISO, general counsel). Then go a level down. VPs and directors in finance, IT, and HR make requests like these every week, so a call from one of them raises fewer eyebrows than a surprise call from the CEO. Add a few outside contacts with real authority over money or access, like a key supplier's accounts receivable lead or the engineer at your managed service provider. The second is the people an attacker would call. Accounts payable, treasury, payroll, HR, executive assistants, the IT help desk, and anyone who can grant or change access in your identity platform. The help desk and the identity admins get left off these lists a lot. They shouldn't be. A cloned voice asking for an MFA reset is a fast route to Account Takeover (ATO). A cloned voice asking for a new admin account skips a few steps. For everyone on the first list, note how much public audio and video exists. Earnings calls, podcast appearances, conference keynotes, webinar recordings, and social media clips all give an attacker training material. A CFO with three hours of recorded keynotes is a much easier clone than one who's never been on camera. It doesn't take three hours, though. A few minutes from a single webinar can be enough, which puts most directors on the list too. What comes out of this step is a short matrix: the identities most worth faking and the people most likely to get their calls. In most organizations that's a few dozen people. Manageable. Step 2. Write the verification rules before testing them A drill without a clear rule only measures instinct. Before running any scenario, document what employees are supposed to do. Strong verification rules tend to share a few traits. Out-of-band callback. Any request to move money, change bank details, share credentials, reset MFA, or change who has access to what gets confirmed through a number pulled from the internal directory or vendor master file. Never a number supplied in the request itself. Clear thresholds. Spell out which actions always require verification, no matter who's asking or how urgent it sounds. Dual approval. Two people sign off on new payees, changed banking details, new privileged accounts, and role changes. Challenge phrases. The most-impersonated executives and their direct support staff share a phrase that rotates on a schedule. No-blame reporting. Anyone who realizes they already acted on a suspicious request (paid it, reset it, granted it) reports it right away, and nobody gets shamed for it. Shame the first person who comes forward and the next one with that sinking feeling keeps quiet while the attacker keeps working. Explicit permission to pause. The CEO and CFO tell their teams, in writing, that nobody gets in trouble for hanging up and calling back. Don't skip that last one. Deepfake fraud runs on urgency and hierarchy. An employee who thinks slowing down a VP will cost them at review time is the easiest target in the building. So tell people to trust their gut. The voice can be perfect and the request can still feel wrong, and that feeling is worth listening to even when they can't explain it. My advice to every team I talk to: don't just do something, stand there. A minute of standing still and one callback costs nothing. Acting on the fake costs a lot more. Step 3. Design multi-channel scenarios Real attacks rarely show up as a single phone call. They usually start in email or chat to set up context, then move to voice or video to apply pressure. Drill scenarios should follow the same path. Before building anything, get sign-off from legal, HR, and every executive whose identity will be used. Cloning someone's voice without consent creates its own set of problems. Many teams use a consenting executive's voice, a clearly labeled synthetic stand-in, or a live actor working from a script. Four starter scenarios cover most of the risk. Urgent wire from the CFO. A spoofed email flags a confidential acquisition payment, followed by a voicemail in the CFO's voice asking the controller to process it before end of day. Supplier bank change. A message from a known vendor contact announces new banking details, followed by a Microsoft Teams call from the "vendor" to confirm the update. Help desk reset. A caller who sounds exactly like the VP of sales says she's traveling, locked out, and needs MFA moved to a new phone before a board meeting. Access cleanup. An email from the CISO's office announces a quarterly permissions review. Then a Teams call from the "IT director" walks an identity admin through it. Strip excess rights from five users who don't need them, and while you're in there, add a contractor account to a privileged group for the auditors. The cleanup is good hygiene. The one addition is the attack. Time the scenarios around the same pressure points attackers pick. Quarter close, audit season, the days before a holiday, and weeks when executives are publicly known to be on the road. Step 4. Run it in stages Start with a tabletop exercise. Walk the target group through each scenario in a conference room and ask what they'd do at every step. It surfaces policy gaps cheaply. (Someone almost always asks which number they're supposed to call, and nobody in the room is sure.) Then move to live simulations with a small group. A few ground rules keep it safe. Brief a small control group. The executive sponsor, the SOC lead, and the head of finance should know the drill is running so a real escalation doesn't kick off a real incident response. Keep money and access out of reach. Use a test payee, a payment request that stops at approval, and a sandbox group with no real privileges. Nothing real should be able to move. Set stop conditions. If a participant gets distressed or the scenario starts bleeding into real business, end it and debrief on the spot. Tell participants afterward, every time. A drill that feels like a trap burns the trust the whole program depends on. Step 5. Measure what actually happened A single pass/fail score is the least useful number a drill produces. The behaviors underneath it tell security teams far more. Verification rate. The share of participants who used the documented callback or challenge step before acting. Time to escalation. How long it took someone to report the request to security, if anyone did. Report path. Whether the report reached the SOC through the expected channel or stalled in a manager's inbox. Break points. The exact step where the process failed. No directory number, an unclear threshold, or the "executive" pushing to skip the callback. Bundled requests. In the access scenario, whether anyone questioned the privilege grant tucked inside the cleanup, or approved the whole batch because most of it looked right. Trust signals cited. What participants say convinced them. "It sounded exactly like him" and "the email came first, so I assumed it was real" point to very different fixes. Spend the most time on the break points. Each one maps to a specific fix in policy, tooling, or training. Step 6. Debrief, fix, and repeat Keep debriefs blameless and fast, ideally the same day. Most people who fall for a good drill feel lousy about it. Tell them it was built to fool them, because it was. Then walk participants through what was fake, how it was built, and which signals they could have checked. Fix what broke. Update the callback directory, tighten thresholds, and fold the scenarios into the regular phishing simulation program so the lessons don't fade after one round. Repeat the drill at least twice a year, and any time the high-exposure list changes. A new CFO, an acquisition, or a heavy conference season all count. Rotate scenarios so nobody passes by recognizing the script. Where technology fits Process carries most of the load. Tooling helps at two points in the attack chain. The first is the setup message. Most voice and video deepfake attempts are preceded by an email or chat message that establishes context. Behavioral email security that flags unusual requests from executives, managers, or vendor contacts can break the chain before the call ever happens. The second is the call itself. Real-time identity verification for collaboration platforms like Microsoft Teams analyzes voice and video during a meeting and warns participants when someone doesn't match the identity they claim. Many detection tools look for artifacts, the glitches a generator leaves behind, and those get harder to spot with every model release. A sturdier approach checks the person, comparing behavioral and biometric signals against a profile of the real speaker. When evaluating these tools, look closely at privacy, specifically whether they record or transcribe meetings or only process signals in the moment. IRONSCALES, the first and only email security platform with deepfake protection built into the product, takes the behavioral and biometric route for Microsoft Teams meetings. It works from mathematical voice and face profiles, with no recordings or transcripts kept. Start small, start this quarter A first drill doesn't need a budget line. Two lists, one page of verification rules, four scenarios, and a debrief template are enough to learn where you actually stand. For finance and compliance teams that want more detail on warning signs, FinCEN's alert on deepfake fraud schemes describes criminals using generative AI to impersonate executives and direct employees to transfer funds. One of its red flags is worth building straight into the drill. Watch for anyone who switches communication methods mid-conversation and blames technical glitches. That "bad connection" from the CFO on a Friday afternoon is exactly the moment to hang up and call back. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Audian Paxson, Principal Technical Strategist, IRONSCALES.

zrpvce.text: A new Android malware called Hirudo steals bank account credentials by replacing legitimate banking apps with modified versions that disable security checks. Researchers identified malicious copies of eight banking apps that use a hooking engine to bypass app-signature, Accessibility, and Play Integrity checks by substituting certificate information or returning empty lists. Threat actors can use Hirudo to steal credentials, remotely control infected phones in real time, collect messages, capture screenshots, and record audio. A report today from mobile security company ThreatFabric notes that Hirudo has been observed impersonating at least seven Indonesian banks, but the malware also targets financial organizations in China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand. The malware is typically delivered via apps for shopping (Shopora), adult content (1V1 X), or short drama (ZoyaTV, KoiShort) that appear legitimate and provide the promised functionality. The researchers say that these apps act as malware loaders for Hirudo, showing a fake “update” notification that leads to permission-granting prompts, including for Accessibility services Overview of the attack chainSource: ThreatFabric Once installed, Hirudo launches the real banking app’s uninstaller, downloads a patched copy, and abuses its Accessibility permission to install it. ThreatFabric explains that this is a delicate, risky process for the malware, since the victim can interrupt it at two points. The app replacement processSource: ThreatFabric ThreatFabric found that the malicious copy of a banking app retains almost all of the original app’s code, but loads a hooking engine built on the open-source frameworks YAHFA and Dobby. When launched, the patched app performs the following evasion actions: Substitute the genuine signing certificate when queried. Hide enabled Accessibility services. Remove screenshot protection, allowing remote viewing and recording. Modify key-attestation certificates and relay Play Integrity requests through an operator-controlled server. “With the engine running inside the banking app's own process, the app's defenses are turned against it,” the researchers say. Evasion methodsSource: ThreatFabric However, ThreatFabric explains there are certain limitations to these evasion methods. The bundled attestation keybox has been publicly leaked, and Google lists two of its certificates as compromised, so server-side revocation checks can detect those forgeries. Once active on the device, Hirudo can steal banking passwords, payment PINs, device-unlock secrets, and SMS messages, stream the screen to operators, and provide access to both cameras. The malware’s fake checkout pages collect payment PINs, then display a fabricated payment-success result to deceive victims while it steals data. Stealing the victim's PINSource: ThreatFabric ThreatFabric found that Hirudo currently targets Indonesian banking apps and found thousands of application-credential entries in an unsecured backend panel, along with device, lock-screen, and financial-profile data. However, the victim count remains unknown. According to the researchers, “Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications,” shifting the focus from device-level integrity checks to the security mechanisms built into banking apps. The researchers suggest that banks should validate integrity and attestation server-side, bind checks to sessions and protected actions, and retain behavioral and transaction-risk controls. Android users are strongly recommended to keep their devices up-to-date, avoid installing APK files sourced from unofficial Android stores, and periodically run Play Protect scans. Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed. Save your seat

q2tk1o.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 14, 2026Vulnerability / Browser Security A team at security firm XBOW chained three then-unknown Google Chrome bugs into a single attack that runs code on a Windows computer when the user only loads a web page, the company said. Its researchers built the attack in six days by directing AI agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. Google has since confirmed all three bugs, fixed them, and paid XBOW its top $250,000 reward for a full Chrome exploit. The attack is a full chain: a set of bugs used together to break every layer of Chrome's protection, from a web page all the way to the computer. Chrome runs web page code inside two nested sandboxes, the barriers that stop a hacked page from reaching the rest of the machine. The chain crossed both. The result was code running outside Chrome on Windows, with no need for the user to click or download anything. All three bugs are now fixed, and XBOW says they were never used against Chrome users. The two that carry public identifiers were fixed in Chrome 152.0.7977.65 on August 25 and 152.0.7977.82 on September 3. Chrome updates on its own, but the fix only takes effect after the browser restarts, so the action is to relaunch Chrome and confirm the version is 152.0.7977.82 or later. The six days are the headline, and they need their frame. XBOW built the awarded chain between Sunday, August 2, and Friday, August 7, during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences in Las Vegas. That sprint followed months of earlier work: the company set the challenge at a January staff meeting in Malta, and its first full Chrome chain took two months to complete. One version of the awarded chain nearly failed when a bug it relied on turned out to be one Google already knew about. XBOW had built the exploit in swappable parts with backups ready, so it replaced that part and the chain held. By the company's own count of its usage logs, the six-day run cost about $40,000 in AI charges. XBOW also drew a line between what the AI did and what people did. The AI agents searched Chrome's source code, tested ideas, built proofs of concept, and wrote the first drafts of the exploit. The researchers chose the targets, supplied context, challenged the agents' results, and decided which pieces to join. One researcher, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, built the awarded chain with the agents. "Pre-LLMs a Chrome full chain would take a team of four around 6-9 months to be produced, our first submission took 2 months. The awarded one? six days," Dolan-Gavitt wrote. The three bugs each sat in a different part of Chrome. Google's own release notes credit Dolan-Gavitt of XBOW for two of them and list the version that fixed each. Stage Where CVE Fixed in 1 V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine CVE-2026-85045 152.0.7977.82 (Sep 3) 2 Animated-WebP image decoder No public identifier listed Chrome 152 cycle 3 Crashpad, Chrome's crash handler CVE-2026-78952 152.0.7977.65 (Aug 25) The first bug gave the attacker control of memory inside Chrome's JavaScript engine. The second, in the code that reads animated WebP images, used that control to break out of the engine's inner sandbox and make one precise write to the computer's memory. The third, in Crashpad, Chrome's crash handler, which runs outside the sandbox, turned that single write into full code execution on the machine. Both identified bugs are rated high severity and need the user to load a page. The WebP bug was fixed in the same Chrome 152 cycle, but no public identifier can be confirmed for it: the one XBOW's announcement gives the WebP stage, CVE-2026-85045, is the identifier Google and XBOW's own technical write-up both assign to the V8 bug. Google's Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program pays up to $250,000 for a full-chain exploit, the most it offers for a single report, under rules it updated in 2026. It awards at most four of these a year. XBOW calls this the first full-chain Chrome reward under the 2026 rules and the first to an autonomous security company. Before the fixes shipped, the bugs put an estimated 1 billion people running Chrome on Windows at risk of this kind of attack, according to the company. XBOW's point is the speed. "It only took an estimated $40,000 of compute and six days for a single researcher to produce a chain that previously would have taken months," founder Oege de Moor said in the announcement. Dolan-Gavitt put the warning for defenders plainly: "Six days and $40k is not a lot of time or money when the payoff is a Chrome chain!" The bar, he wrote, is now much lower. "Defend accordingly."

1gdb2yz.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that works by replacing legitimate banking apps with purpose-built patched versions designed to bypass security checks from inside the app itself, marking a new escalation in financial fraud. Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it identified replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while credential targeting in the malware spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand. "The operation combines credential theft, device takeover, screen and camera capture, and SMS theft, in combination with a fairly mature backend," Eward Driehuis, vice president of fraud engineering at ThreatFabric, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. Hirudo facilitates on-device credential theft and live remote control. The malware is delivered by shopping, adult video, and entertainment dropper apps that carry the trojan as a separate installation package, which is then served as an in-app update. Some of the dropper apps are listed below - Shopora (com.agbbh.kjdrttt) 1V1 X (com.onev.vip) KoiShort (com.koishort.app) ZoyaTV (com.zoyatv.app) "The lure is functional, loading real content in a WebView, a storefront, a video catalogue or short dramas, so the experience looks legitimate," ThreatFabric explained. "Behind that content the dropper runs a fixed startup routine: it collects promotion-tracking data, fetches its campaign configuration, and checks whether the payload, the Hirudo RAT, is already installed with its accessibility service and notification access enabled." If it's not present, it displays a fake in-app update prompt to trigger the installation of the malware. It's worth emphasizing that Hirudo is installed as a second app and must be granted its own permissions before it can carry out the malicious activities. As observed in the case of StreamRat, the malware implements an anti-detection technique based on blocking Internet access by configuring a deliberately non-functional VPN connection prior to the payload installation. This is seen as an attempt to prevent other apps and services, like Google Play Protect, from carrying out cloud-based checks of the payload. "However, Play Protect also provides offline detection for known potentially harmful applications, meaning that the mechanism does not completely disable its protection," ThreatFabric noted last month. "We therefore assess that the technique is more likely intended to reduce the effectiveness of online reputation and code-analysis mechanisms rather than bypass Play Protect entirely." Depending on the nature of the lure app used, the dropper is also designed to serve bogus screens to capture payment PINs, serve fake screens requesting login credentials for banks and wallet apps, display fake lock screen pattern and PIN overlays, and facilitate total remote control of the device. While all this behavior is par for the course when it comes to Android banking trojans, it's their attempts to replace the target banking app with a tampered copy that stand out. Specifically, the purpose-built replacements embed a hooking engine to blind signature, accessibility, screen-capture, and Play Integrity checks from within the app. The replacement targets eight Indonesian apps. "For these, the RAT detects the installed banking app through accessibility, checks its signing certificate against a stored reference, [and] then shows a fake 'update' prompt," ThreatFabric explained. "It opens Android's uninstaller for the genuine app without waiting for the user to tap, and downloads the bank-specific replacement in parallel." While the need for having to remove the app before installing its near-identical malicious copy is a "real constraint," the mechanism offers the ability to bypass the banking app's own security checks by returning responses fed by the attacker beforehand. This involves returning the genuine app signing certificate, returning an empty list when querying for enabled accessibility services, and stripping the FLAG_SECURE flag so that the app's screens can be viewed and recorded remotely. "Key-attestation certificates are re-signed with a bundled keybox, and Play Integrity requests are relayed over plain HTTP to an operator-controlled server, which returns a verdict for the app to accept," the mobile security company said. "Two details are worth underlining for defenders. First, the attestation keybox the engine ships is not the operators' own: it is a publicly leaked keybox. Second, because the Integrity request is relayed rather than genuinely produced, a valid Integrity response alone is not evidence of an untampered app." Evidence indicates that the malware is distributed via fake web pages masquerading as Google Play Store landing pages for shopping, short drama, and football apps. Unsuspecting users are assessed to be directed to these websites through ads on Meta-owned social media platforms. The entire operation rests on a backend that combines device control with the ability to manage different campaigns and stolen data, including device records, lock-screen history, and financial profiles containing monthly income and risk-score fields. "Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications," ThreatFabric said. "By moving its tampering inside the target app, the operation shifts the contest from the device to the application's own integrity checks, and from a bespoke patch to a reusable engine that can be retargeted at other apps and regions." "Once an app can be replaced, its locally produced signals, signature, accessibility list, and integrity verdict, must be treated as attacker-influenced and verified server-side," ThreatFabric said. Last month, the findings came a little over a month after the cybersecurity firm revealed StreamRat's targeting of Spanish-speaking users via Meta and TikTok advertisements impersonating a free TV streaming service named Streamtv Esp to enable control over compromised Android devices. "StreamRat abuses accessibility services and MediaProjection to provide operators with near-complete control over infected devices, combining VNC and hidden-screen control, UI-tree collection, keylogging, credential-stealing overlays, internet and screen-blocking capabilities," ThreatFabric said.

1t503wm.text: The bug was simple: the login let you choose where your sign-in code went. Proving it on a live website was the hard part. TL;DR During an authorized assessment, an AI pentesting agent found a critical authentication bypass on a major insurer's production website, on its own. One login request let the user choose where the one-time passcode went. The attack was the easy part. Proving it on a live site took web context built over a decade. The Login Worked. Then the Agent Stopped. Reflectiz's AI pentesting agent was mapping the login flow of a major insurer's production website, which has millions of users. The agent requested a login code and directed it to an email inbox it controlled. The code arrived. The login went through. Its guardrails halted the test after the login succeeded. The agent had discovered a critical-severity authentication bypass on its own. Reflectiz reported it to the insurer. The Flaw: The Request Chose Where the Code Went A one-time passcode (OTP) only proves who you are if it goes somewhere already linked to the account. Here, that link was broken. The login request carried two fields that decided delivery: the channel and the address. Normally, the code went by text to the phone number on the account. But the request could change the channel. Switch it to email, and the server sent the code to whatever address the request named, not the address registered to the account. Simplified, the request looked like this: The server never checked that the address belonged to the account. Binding a code to its account is one of the most basic checks in authentication. OWASP's testing guide asks this in plain words: "Are the OTPs tied to the correct user account...?" An attacker with the required customer identifiers could potentially use the flaw to access that customer's account. From a Suspicious Field to a Proven Bypass The agent began with reconnaissance, looking at the site's JavaScript and the API calls behind its pages. That analysis surfaced the OTP request and two values that appeared to control how and where the code was sent. Values like those can suggest a hypothesis, but they’re not a finding, since the server might reject the changes or block them later in the login. So the agent built a targeted test around both values and ran it through the live login flow, which confirmed the bypass. Illustration of the authenticated state the agent reached before stopping. Recreated and anonymized. Want to see how that testing process works? Book a technical demo to examine how Reflectiz investigates website workflows, validates findings, and controls execution. Web Context Is the Hard Part Plenty of automated testing stops at the login gate, but much of what matters sits behind it. A testing system that cannot reach a workflow cannot assess what happens inside it. Reflectiz solved that problem long before the agent existed. The company has spent more than a decade scanning thousands of production websites, which meant logging in, receiving verification codes, and navigating multi-step flows. So, on sites the company already monitors, the agent starts with that context instead of a blank URL. Reflectiz's agentic pentesting puts that web context to work. It drives a real browser through the flows a customer follows, including one-time passcodes and 2FA. Reflectiz CTO and co-founder Ysrael Gurt, a longtime ethical hacker, built the agent on that foundation. One Finding Is Not a Coverage Report A confirmed vulnerability may show what failed, but it doesn’t show how much of the application was tested. The OTP test ran alongside other attack plans on the same site. Reflectiz's agentic pentesting pairs that open-ended investigation with a structured plan: test every discovered endpoint against every applicable attack category. A separate validator agent reproduces each suspected finding with the same payload and context before it is reported. The output is a coverage record of which tests ran, their recorded outcomes, and any exclusions. Pentested Is Not the Same as Secure The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier. This assessment found an exploitable login flaw, though it is unclear when the weakness was introduced. That is not a reflection on human testers, because a skilled tester could have found this flaw too. It’s more a reflection on the nature of point-in-time testing. It has its place, but how often can anyone afford to look? Websites change with every release, but pentest schedules don't. They’re rigid, which isn’t much use against attackers who now use AI to find flaws fast and won’t wait for the next test window. Agentic testing keeps pace. It can repeat focused tests as often as the site changes, provided the agent has the right access and clear boundaries, and produces evidence a reviewer can verify. Reflectiz reports up to 10x the testing capacity at the same operational cost as traditional manual pentesting. The comparison concerns testing volume, rather than a guarantee of 10x more vulnerabilities found. In the demo, ask how scope, testing depth, and frequency affect capacity and cost for your applications. Bring Your Toughest Website Workflow to the Demo Book a 30-minute technical demo with a Reflectiz web security specialist. Before the demo, think about a workflow that matters to your business. It could be login, account recovery, checkout, or a customer portal. During the demo you can then review: How the agent navigates authenticated, multi-step workflows What evidence it finds to support a validated finding How scope, guardrails, and coverage are documented Discuss your application's requirements and what a first assessment would involve. No commitment is required, and there’s no need to test your website during the walkthrough. Book your agentic pentesting demo

42qis2.text: Microsoft has confirmed that non-admin users may be unable to connect to devices via Remote Desktop after installing recent Windows updates if the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled. This feature began rolling out with the KB5067036 preview cumulative update to systems running Windows 11 24H2/25H2 in October 2025, and it is now enabled by default in organizations using Windows security baselines after installing the October 2026 Windows security update. When toggled on, admin protection ensures logged-in users have only standard user permissions and prompts them to authenticate via Windows Hello (PIN or biometric) when they try to install new apps or change the Windows registry. On Tuesday, Microsoft confirmed that Remote Desktop connections may fail with error 0xC000000D after installing the KB5124010 September 2026 non-security preview update or later updates on systems running Windows 11 24H2/25H2/26H1/26H2. "Attempts to connect might fail with error 0xC000000D and display the message, 'The token that was passed to the function is invalid.' This issue primarily affects enterprise-managed remote devices used as Remote Desktop hosts with Administrator protection enabled, regardless of how the feature was enabled," it said. "If your organization uses Windows security baselines, published through the Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit, Administrator protection is enabled by default in Windows 11, version 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 security baselines, unless your organization has configured the policy differently." While the company continues to work on this issue, it has shared a temporary workaround that requires IT admins to disable Administrator protection through a policy management method of their choice. For instance, if you use Microsoft Intune or Group Policy, you'll need to reset the "User Account Control Type Of Admin Approval Mode" policy. Microsoft fixed a similar issue in March 2025 that caused Remote Desktop and RDS connection failures after installing Windows updates released since January 2025. Last month, it also released emergency out-of-band Windows updates to fix Remote Desktop Services failures on Windows Server devices caused by the September 2026 security updates. 11nd7ks.text: A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet. vhost is the part of the Linux kernel that speeds up network and other input/output for virtual machines and containers. A local user reaches it by opening a device node, usually /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. On the host, the flaw gives an unprivileged user a reliable way to read and write any kernel address, bypass KASLR, and escalate to root. The attack is deterministic: it needs no memory grooming and no lucky timing. The second attack is narrower. When a virtual machine's virtio device is placed behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform turned on, and vhost runs in device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can trigger the same bug and make the host kernel write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it. How it works vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live. With a device IOTLB attached, those commands accept the new addresses without checking them, leaving that check for later. Once the cache is filled, the subsequent check never runs, and vhost continues translating new addresses using the old mapping. The kernel then copies data to or from that pointer without a bounds check, so a write to the used ring or a read of a descriptor lands outside the mapped region. That gives the attacker kernel read and write. The flaw sat in the code for about nine years because it took two reasonable changes to create it. A 2017 change (Linux 4.11) added the cache and its shortcut. A 2020 change (Linux 5.9) moved address checking out of the command and into a later step, removing the check that would otherwise have caught the stale translation. Who is affected, and what to do The flaw affects Linux kernels from 4.11 up to 7.2-rc4. Tencent reproduced the full local-user-to-root chain on five distribution kernels: Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node was limited to the kvm group, so the starting point there was a member of that group rather than any user. On the other four tested images, the node was world-readable at mode 0666, so any local user could reach it. The fix (commit de845981da67) clears the cache whenever the ring is reconfigured. Install a kernel that contains it and reboot. The first fixed upstream stable releases are listed below; vendors may also backport the fix without changing their version number. Stable branch First fixed version 5.10.y 5.10.265 5.15.y 5.15.216 6.1.y 6.1.183 6.6.y 6.6.152 6.12.y 6.12.104 6.18.y 6.18.45 7.1.y 7.1.9 7.2 7.2 Red Hat, Amazon Linux, and Oracle Linux have shipped fixes. Ubuntu has fixed 22.04 and, as of October 13, still lists its 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as in progress. Until a fixed kernel is in place, restrict access to the vhost device nodes. Remove world access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock, limit the owning group to trusted virtualization services, and treat membership in that group as a privilege while the vulnerable kernel is running. There is no interim workaround for the guest-to-host escape; for that path, the patched kernel is the only remedy. The severity, and the AI finder The flaw is rated high, not critical, and the raters disagree on how high. The kernel.org CVE team scores it 8.8 and marks its scope as changed, because the guest-to-host write reaches memory in the host's QEMU process and crosses the boundary between a guest and its host. Red Hat scores it at 7.3 and marks the scope as unchanged, treating the impact as remaining within the host's own trust boundary; it also rates the integrity impact lower. Amazon scored it 7.8 and Oracle 7.3. The bug was found with help from Corvus AI, a multi-agent system Tencent built for kernel vulnerability research. The upstream fix credits it with an Assisted-by line, and Tencent says the pipeline found the flaw. This is machine-assisted research, not an attack run by AI. It is the same team and pipeline behind an 18-year-old SCTP kernel flaw disclosed in August, which also reached root and, in testing, escaped a container.

1au16uj.text: Security researchers ran their own code inside a protected part of Windows that is meant to stay sealed off even when the rest of the computer is taken over. The protected area is a VBS enclave, an isolated slice of memory the operating system uses to guard secrets, and the one they broke into handles passwords for a Windows anti-phishing feature. The work was done in a lab as a proof of concept, has not been seen in real attacks, and Microsoft fixed the flaw in its September 8, 2026 update. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-83498. Microsoft rates it an elevation-of-privilege issue, Critical, with a CVSS score of 7.8, and says it has not been exploited and was not publicly known before the fix. Microsoft also says it found the same issue internally. The research, by the security firm Doyensec, was published October 13, more than a month after the patch. A VBS enclave is a signed library that a normal Windows program loads but cannot read or change once it is running. The Windows hypervisor keeps the enclave's memory in a more trusted world, called VTL1 or Isolated User Mode, that ordinary code in the normal world, VTL0, cannot reach, according to Microsoft. The design is meant to protect what is inside even if an attacker has already taken over the normal kernel or is running as SYSTEM. Running attacker-chosen code inside that world is what makes this research notable. The enclave Doyensec attacked is SFAPE.dll, the component behind Enhanced Phishing Protection in Microsoft Defender SmartScreen. That feature watches text you type or paste and warns you if you enter your Windows sign-in password into an unsafe place, such as Notepad or a phishing page. To do this without exposing the password, Windows intercepts it at login and stores it in hashed form within the enclave, so later inputs can be checked against it. On a Windows 11 system, the program that loads this enclave is lsass.exe, the process that handles sign-in credentials and runs as SYSTEM. The attack does not work from a distance. It needs a program already running on the machine that loads and calls the enclave; for SFAPE, that's LSASS. Microsoft's own rating says the same: the attack vector is local, and the attacker needs low-level access and no help from the user. In short, this is a way for code that already has a foothold to reach into the more trusted world next to it, not a way in from outside. Doyensec built the attack from a small mistake and widened it step by step. Calling the enclave's Initialize function a second time makes it write a fixed four-byte error value to an address the calling program controls, and this time it skips the address check the first call performs. Doyensec is clear that this alone is weak, writing that calling it an arbitrary write "would be a huge overstatement." Aimed at the right spot, though, that one write corrupts the value the enclave uses to tell its own memory from the host's, so its safety check stops working. From there, a timing bug in another function triggers a controlled wipe. That wipe redirects how the enclave looks up a stored object, and the resulting read and write let the researchers replace the table that decides which code the enclave may run. The result is attacker-chosen code running inside the enclave. The work broke the enclave's isolation; it did not show that a user's password was read or stolen, and Microsoft's advisory describes the impact as data leakage from or code execution inside the enclave. Microsoft fixed the flaw in the September 8, 2026 cumulative update, KB5124008, for Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2. Doyensec compared the old and new files and found the patched enclave now checks the address before that first write and tightens the function the timing bug relied on. The update also ships a new policy that prevents the old, vulnerable enclave from loading at all, so a patched system cannot run it. There is no separate workaround to apply; installing the update is the action. One gap outlives this fix. Windows has no general blocklist for vulnerable enclaves like the one it keeps for vulnerable drivers, and the September policy only blocks the old SFAPE file. An older Microsoft Edge enclave with a similar read-and-write flaw, CVE-2023-36880 from 2023, is still allowed to load, Doyensec said. Whether that was a deliberate choice or an oversight is unclear. That matters because loading a signed but flawed enclave is a known trick, sometimes called "bring your own vulnerable enclave," that earlier research from Akamai and Outflank used to hide code and data from security tools. Blocking one flawed enclave while leaving another loadable leaves that trick available.

c6rdh7.text: Microsoft on Tuesday shattered its own Patch Tuesday record by shipping patches for a whopping 1,413 vulnerabilities, including one that it said has come under active exploitation. These include 1,102 flaws in Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server. Of these, more than 670 relate to privilege escalation, followed by over 300 remote code execution flaws and 250 information disclosure flaws. Over 70 flaws are rated Critical in severity. "Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it's the baseline," Dustin Childs, head of Threat Awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), said. "Is AI to blame? Partly. It's accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too." "But AI isn't creating these bugs out of thin air; it's just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it. The volume isn't the real story anymore. What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what's proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month's new normal." The three vulnerabilities of note are listed below - CVE-2026-96951 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A command injection vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network. CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An untrusted search path vulnerability in .NET Framework that allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally. CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An improperly controlled sequential memory allocation vulnerability in MessagePack-CSharp that allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network. Microsoft, which credited Fujitsu's Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo, as well as Anthropic's Benoit Sevens and a researcher named yhw for reporting CVE-2026-96951, said the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. "An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could evade Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses," the Windows-maker said. "In an email or instant message attack scenario, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file that is designed to exploit the vulnerability." "In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment." It's unclear how the vulnerability is being exploited in real-world attacks, by whom, and who has been targeted. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 16, 2026. CVE-2026-108398 has been acknowledged as publicly known at the time of the release of the patches, with Microsoft stating the security flaw could be exploited to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement and run unauthorized applications on target systems. "An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process," Microsoft said. "Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required." "This vulnerability is particularly dangerous as a post-compromise attack technique, enabling attackers with existing local access to circumvent security restrictions without user interaction," Mike Walters, president and co-founder of Action1, said. "Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity, expose sensitive business information, weaken endpoint defenses, and disrupt critical operations." Microsoft attributed the vulnerability discovery to James Forshaw with Google Project Zero, while crediting an anonymous researcher for reporting CVE-2026-92707. The security flaw is the second to be tagged as publicly disclosed. Patches have also been released for a non-Microsoft CVE (CVE-2026-21413, CVSS score: 9.8), a heap-based buffer overflow impacting Raw Image Extension that could result in remote code execution. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to navigate to a folder containing a specially crafted RAW image file," Microsoft said. "The vulnerability can be triggered when Windows generates a thumbnail or preview; the user does not need to open the file." The development comes amid continued use of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches to discover and remediate security vulnerabilities. Last month, Microsoft addressed nearly 1,000 vulnerabilities. According to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, more than 4,000 CVEs have been patched by Microsoft this year alone. "The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower," Adam Barnett, Lead Software Engineer at Rapid7, said. Along with this month's updates, Redmond has also introduced a new method to help organizations prioritize security updates by grouping related flaws into what it calls "risk cohorts." "A risk cohort is a group of CVEs that require a similar customer assessment," Microsoft said. "Risk cohorts are a starting point, not a final decision. Customers should continue to review each CVE for active exploitation, severity, attack vector, user interaction, and product-specific guidance."

hv28i0.text: A Saudi National and employee of OpenAI has been arrested for allegedly planting a hidden recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco offices to covertly record sensitive conversations. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He was arrested by authorities on October 9, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Alfozan had been employed at OpenAI since July 2025, working as an engineering lead. He has since been terminated. According to Alfozan's LinkedIn profile, he graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, with a master's in data science in 2025. He was previously employed at Meta as a senior systems engineer and went on to become the founding engineer at Nash. "Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," Kash Patel, Director of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a statement. "Protecting American SI [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities." According to the complaint, on or around September 30, 2026, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room. The device was said to have been concealed in toilet paper and installed sometime around September 28, 2026. Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage obtained from within OpenAI's office showed Alfozan appearing near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the discovery despite having no authority to access or participate in meetings taking place in the executive conference room. The room, the complaint added, was reserved for discussions involving "highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships." Prior to the installation of the recording device, Alfozan is also alleged to have used an unspecified productivity tool to gather details about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, "leadership and exec" locations, and external partner meetings. On top of that, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse was allegedly used to submit various prompts between September 24 and 30, 2026, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device. Some of these prompts are listed below - Build a continuous audio recorder Customize Wi-Fi ... connectivity Improve audio and live listening Encrypt the SD card The same chatbot account is also said to have submitted prompts related to the device, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between September 27 and 28, 2026. Then on October 5, 2026, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which the device was inserted. On the same day, Alfozan allegedly left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building, which contained a second recording device, along with his wallet and ID. In a statement shared on X, OpenAI said it discovered a sophisticated recording device, and that it used its own artificial intelligence (AI) models to "understand the device and where it had come from," adding it referred the matter to the FBI after discovering an employee had planted it. It's unclear what made the device "sophisticated," but OpenAI told TechCrunch that it contained "advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring." "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the ChatGPT-maker said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats." If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release. The development comes as OpenAI fired three safety researchers earlier this month after an investigation found they had violated company policies ​on handling sensitive information.

According to the DOJ, OpenAI determined that the device had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28, and contained encrypted data. "On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco," says the DOJ press release. Spy device found in OpenAI executive conference roomSource: DOJ The DOJ says the conference room was regularly used for meetings involving confidential information about OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, technical capabilities, business relationships, and government engagements. lyrkxt.text: A critical heap buffer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-39919) in the Ghostscript interpreter and rendering engine could allow remote code execution through specially crafted PDF files. The flaw was discovered on August 23 by researchers at Defiant's platform Wordfence using their Argus AI-powered system. Ghostscript is a PostScript and PDF interpreter that can render PDFs as images, generate thumbnails for previews, and optimize PDF files by compressing embedded images and removing unnecessary font data. When generating a PDF thumbnail, WordPress can use the PHP Imagick extension to call ImageMagick, which launches Ghostscript. A specially crafted PDF file containing a JPEG 2000 image can trigger incorrect handling of low-bit-depth samples and mismatched component resolutions. Using Argus, the researchers developed two exploits for CVE-2026-39919 that force Ghostscript to write 1,024 bytes into a 256-byte buffer, corrupting nearby memory and leading to unauthenticated remote code execution in a WordPress deployment. Wordfence focused on WordPress systems, but notes that the flaw affects any online system running Ghostscript 9.21 through 10.07.1 and is exploitable if the payload is adjusted to the environment. The researchers tested ten Linux environments, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Alpine, and AlmaLinux, as well as an official WordPress Docker image snapshot, and found that all contained the vulnerable code. Tested environmentsSource: Wordfence The researchers tested two proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits and found that their ability to trigger the vulnerability depended on the target environment. In a lab testbed, they executed the exploits 10,240 times against Linux packages but failed to achieve remote code execution. However, they successfully executed code remotely on a purpose-built test server. The researchers found that modifying the PDF's fonts, language settings, font configuration, and one core system library enabled the exploit to succeed, although not reliably. In WordPress environments specifically, successful exploitation has four prerequisites: An attacker can upload a PDF, anonymously or through a low-privileged account. The site processes that PDF to generate a preview or thumbnail. The processing chain reaches Ghostscript, with the necessary software and policy settings permitting PDF rendering. Ghostscript contains the unpatched vulnerable decoding code. Wordfence noted that stock WordPress does not permit anonymous Media Library uploads. More generally, any application that renders attacker-supplied PDFs through affected Ghostscript code may expose the flaw, and authentication requirements for exploitation depend on the application. Artifex, the maintainer of Ghostscript, rolled out a fix on September 8, in version 10.08.0 of the interpreter. Fixes were also backported to older versions, so users should check the revision details for patch status. WordPress administrators need to ensure, through their hosting provider, that Ghostscript has been upgraded to version 10.08.0 or later. If using Docker, it is recommended to rebuild and redeploy with an updated, patched base image. If unable to upgrade to a fixed Ghostscript release, it is recommended to block PDF uploads to the server or disable PDF rendering in ImageMagick. Wordfence said it has not seen any in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-39919 yet. 13n8bmr.text: Anthropic is warning that small AI models could soon be able to self-replicate across consumer IoT devices, from Android TV boxes to smart ovens, creating distributed botnets capable of running AI workloads without relying on data centers. The company's experiments showed that models could identify unfamiliar devices, connect them into a network, and prepare them to run an AI model. Although the researchers successfully distributed the Gemma4-26B-A4B model from Google DeepMind on 15 off-brand Android TV boxes, they did not demonstrate a fully autonomous, self-replicating AI worm running on real IoT hardware. However, they estimate that smaller models could achieve self-replication by the end of the year if they continue to improve at their historical rate. “Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes,” Anthropic warns. “ A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days).” Small AI model powerSource: Anthropic Replication experiment Anthropic ran its replication experiment using cheap Android TV boxes, and the AI models Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-26B-A4B, Llama3.1-8B, Opus 4.8, and GLM-5.2, each assigned a different role. Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.2 acted as agents tasked with setting up and propagating Llama3.1-8B (inference), while Gemma4-26B-A4B demonstrated that a model could run across 15 Android TV boxes. Opus 4.8 was separately tested as an advisor to Qwen. The experiment used a simplified setting where the targets exposed unauthenticated ADB access. Evaluation overviewSource: Anthropic The experiments showed that Qwen3.5-9B successfully installed and configured the software needed to run Llama3.1-8B on eight of the nine hardware types tested. GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in the controlled emulated network in four out of five trials, but the other models failed to complete the full process reliably. Anthropic observed an improvement in success rate when it retained data from previous attempts, with Qwen3.5-9 B's success rate rising from 45% early on to 84% in later generations. Improving iterationsSource: Anthropic Using the stronger Opus 4.8 model to assist Qwen in inference produced no measurable improvement. Based on the results and historical data, Anthropic predicts that models with 30 billion parameters or fewer could reach the necessary capability level by the end of 2026. On the studied hardware, the inference setup would be a slow process, taking between 28 and 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B, and 71-150 hours for Gemma4-26B-A4B, giving defenders enough time to detect and respond. However, this time could shrink with future models, so implementing stronger security measures for IoT may soon become a priority. Proposed defenses include detecting large model transfers and unusual device-to-device traffic, using honeypots to inspect payloads, quarantining infected subscribers, and improving IoT security defaults. While Anthropic’s warning is not based on an imminent threat, as their experiment failed to demonstrate full end-to-end worm-creation capability at this stage, even with lowered security settings and explicit propagation goals, the message for better IoT security remains valid. dhzuvb.text: Today is Microsoft's October 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,411 flaws, including one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.This Patch Tuesday addresses 70 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 57 of which are remote code execution, 11 are elevation of privileges, and 2 are spoofing.When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.Therefore, today's total excludes 348 flaws fixed earlier this month, including vulnerabilities in Azure API Center, Azure App Service, Azure Event Grid, Azure SRE Agent, Mariner, Microsoft Bookings, Microsoft Dataverse, Microsoft Exchange Server, and Microsoft Partner Center.Microsoft announced today that Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of support."Today, October 13, 2026, Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of updates. The October 2026 monthly security update is the last update available for these editions," Microsoft said.Earlier this month, Microsoft also said organizations running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions should upgrade to newer versions as they will no longer receive security updates starting next month.This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.The actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities addressed during this October 2026 Patch Tuesday are:Microsoft patched an actively exploited zero-day security bypass flaw that allowed attackers to bypass the Mark of the Web security feature."Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command ('command injection') in Windows Shell allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network," warns Microsoft.No details have been shared on how attackers exploited the flaw or who disclosed it.Microsoft has fixed a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework that can be exploited to run unauthorized applications."Untrusted search path in .NET Framework allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally," explains Microsoft.Microsoft says this flaw could allow attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement and run unauthorized applications."An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process." Microsoft says."Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required."James Forshaw of Google Project Zero discovered the flaw.Microsoft fixed a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp."Improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network," explains Microsoft.Microsoft has not shared who disclosed the vulnerability.With this month's record-breaking number of vulnerabilities, Microsoft has also introduced a new method for organizations to prioritize security updates by grouping related flaws into what it calls "risk cohorts."The new approach groups similar vulnerabilities together to help organizations better understand which security flaws pose the greatest risk to their systems and should be prioritized for patching.Microsoft stressed that these groups do not necessarily indicate which flaws are the most dangerous, as the actual risk depends on whether they are being exploited in attacks, their severity, and how an organization uses the affected software.Microsoft says the new approach is still experimental and is meant to help organizations prioritize security updates, not replace its existing patching recommendations.Microsoft has published a PDF mapping the October 2026 vulnerabilities to their respective risk cohorts.Below is the complete list of resolved vulnerabilities in the October 2026 updates. Note, this report does include the flaws fixed earlier this month.To access the full description of each vulnerability and the systems it affects, you can view the full report here.
